note: Single-pass extraction (no sentence-level indexing available for this document). Evidence fields reference sections/equations/tables/figures/propositions instead of indexed sentences (S#). Votes/confidence/fidelity fields from the reference schema are omitted since no multi-run validation was performed.

nodes.name: Simple linear/MLP models often beat Transformers in forecasting
nodes.description: A persistent, paradoxical empirical result is that simple linear and MLP-based models often match or outperform Transformer-based forecasters on long-horizon benchmarks.

nodes.name: Standard attention forms convex combinations of inputs
nodes.description: Standard self-attention forms each output as a normalized convex combination of input tokens via softmax, enabling flexible input-dependent routing but not directly parameterizing signed transformations over the sequence axis.

nodes.name: Time-series dynamics require global signed operators
nodes.description: Many time-series dynamics are more naturally expressed as global temporal operators (filtering, harmonic continuation, residualization, demixing) that require signed or zero-sum interactions fundamental to classical signal processing.

nodes.name: Mismatch diagnosed as the root cause of the paradox
nodes.description: The gap between simple sequence-mixing models and Transformers is attributed to this mismatch between the softmax attention primitive (convex-combination routing) and the signed-operator structure that time-series dynamics actually require.

nodes.name: Softmax kernel rows lie on the probability simplex
nodes.description: The softmax attention kernel has entries that are nonnegative and sum to 1 in every row unconditionally, regardless of the query/key projections or input, i.e., each row lies in the standard simplex (Sec 3.2).

nodes.name: This is formalized as a simplex-constrained mixing bottleneck
nodes.description: This unconditional row-simplex property is formalized as the simplex-constrained mixing bottleneck, which becomes especially restrictive for operator-driven time-series tasks.

nodes.name: Claim is about inductive bias, not universal impossibility for deep stacks
nodes.description: The claim is not that deep multi-head Transformers are universally incapable of approximating signed behavior, but that the softmax attention primitive imposes an unfavorable inductive bias for operator-driven temporal tasks; this is scoped explicitly to the single-layer, single-head, scalar-value setting for clean isolation of the primitive-level effect.

components.description: Attention as an incomplete dynamic sequence MLP

nodes.name: Static MLP mixer uses a free learned weight matrix
nodes.description: In a static MLP spatial mixer, the output sequence is generated by o = Wmix v, where Wmix is a free, learned N×N weight matrix mixing information across temporal positions.

nodes.name: Softmax attention realizes a dynamically generated mixing matrix
nodes.description: Softmax attention realizes the MLP-mixer view through a specific factorization where the mixing weights are generated dynamically from the input itself via softmax(HW_Q^T W_K H^T).

nodes.name: This factorization is structurally incomplete
nodes.description: The factorization restricts every row of the dynamic mixer to the probability simplex for every input, and though the post-softmax kernel is generically full-rank, the underlying score matrix has rank at most d_h ≪ N, severely constraining how the dynamic mixer can vary as input changes.

nodes.name: Completing the parameterization requires unconstrained signed operators
nodes.description: To complete this factorized parameterization, unconstrained, signed sequence operators are required to supply the static degrees of freedom that the softmax bottleneck removes.

nodes.name: TOA diverges from HyperMLP's causal DPLR framing
nodes.description: While motivated by HyperMLP's reframing of language-model attention as a dynamic MLP, TOA diverges by focusing on continuous oscillatory time-series geometry, using unconstrained full dense mixing matrices rather than causal DPLR structures, and employing Stochastic Operator Regularization to stabilize these dense operators.

components.description: TOA parameterization: dense sandwiching operators S1, S2

nodes.name: Learnable static matrices S1, S2 sandwich the activation
nodes.description: TOA introduces learnable static matrices S1, S2 that sandwich the attention activation on the right of the score matrix: W_mix^TOA(H) = σ(HW_Q^T W_K H^T) S1 S2, with σ a non-saturating, non-normalizing activation.

nodes.name: S1 redistributes similarity profile pre-activation
nodes.description: S1 redistributes each query's similarity profile across key positions before the activation is applied.

nodes.name: Activation breaks row-normalization; S2 supplies signed degrees of freedom
nodes.description: The activation σ breaks the row-normalization constraint of softmax, and S2 then applies a signed, full-rank linear map to the gated similarities before value aggregation, jointly leaving the nonnegative orthant entirely.

nodes.name: Residual parameterization of S1, S2 starts near identity
nodes.description: S1 = I + M1 and S2 = I + M2 for learnable offset matrices M1, M2 initialized at small scale, so at initialization S1, S2 ≈ I, meaning signal transport begins from the identity operator and departs from it only as gradients shape M1, M2 toward task-specific filtering.

nodes.name: Dense N×N mixers are prone to overfitting
nodes.description: A primary challenge in applying dense N×N sequence mixers to time-series tasks is their high propensity to overfit, given typically small/noisy time-series training sets.

nodes.name: Per-forward-pass stochastic dropout on the offset only
nodes.description: SOR samples a random drop rate p~U[0,1) and a Bernoulli mask at each forward pass, applying inverted dropout to the offset M_i only, leaving the residual identity I untouched.

nodes.name: Inverted scaling preserves offset in expectation but variance diverges as p→1
nodes.description: Inverted dropout scaling preserves the offset in expectation, but the per-entry conditional variance diverges as p→1⁻, which is a deliberate design acting as an implicit regularizer discouraging over-reliance on the offset.

nodes.name: Residual identity outside dropout ensures stable fallback
nodes.description: Because the residual identity is added outside the dropout, when the offset collapses (p→1⁻) the operator reduces to the identity, supplying stable signal transport throughout training even under severe regularization.

components.description: Three structural variants of TOA (activation choice)

nodes.name: TOA-Softmax retains row-normalization as an ablation
nodes.description: TOA-Softmax sandwiches the standard softmax with S1, S2 but retains row-normalization; it serves as a strict structural ablation to test whether merely adding S1/S2 degrees of freedom suffices, or whether the simplex constraint itself must be broken.

nodes.name: TOA-ReLU replaces softmax with ReLU for static signed mixing
nodes.description: TOA-ReLU replaces the normalizing softmax with ReLU, removing the row-normalization constraint so that S2 can project the nonnegative similarities into a fully unconstrained, signed space, completing the dual parameterization; it operates in a static regime with one fixed structural pathway per head.

nodes.name: TOA-Gated adds dynamic regime routing via two branches
nodes.description: TOA-Gated doubles the QK head count into left/right groups: a ReLU-gated left branch supplies a nonnegative similarity profile and a softplus-gated right branch supplies a strictly positive sample-dependent gate; their elementwise product forms a dynamically gated mixing kernel before S2's signed linear map.

nodes.name: TOA-Gated addresses TOA-ReLU's inability to adapt structurally to input
nodes.description: TOA-Gated is motivated by the limitation that TOA-ReLU cannot dynamically alter its structural operator based on the input sequence's macroscopic properties, since it relies on a single, fixed structural pathway.

components.description: Formal impossibility result for softmax attention

nodes.name: Proposition 1: softmax cannot realize non-simplex target operators
nodes.description: Proposition 1 proves that for a single-head self-attention layer with scalar values, if a target operator T* has any row outside the simplex, then no choice of query/key projections can make the attention output equal T* applied to the values for all inputs H.

nodes.name: Proof relies on scale-invariance collapsing softmax to uniform
nodes.description: The proof substitutes a scaled input αH and takes α→0+, showing the softmax kernel collapses to the uniform row 1^T/N (since logits scale as α² while values scale linearly), forcing the target row to equal 1^T/N by surjectivity of the value map, contradicting the assumption that the target row lies outside the simplex.

components.description: Five canonical regimes requiring non-simplex operators

nodes.name: Case A: harmonic continuation requires zero-sum rows
nodes.description: Lemma 1 proves that because sampled sinusoids are orthogonal to the DC component, the optimal operator for seasonal/harmonic continuation requires strictly zero-sum rows, unattainable by softmax; Proposition 2 shows TOA's unconstrained mixer natively recovers these kernels.

nodes.name: Case B: filtering/residualization requires negative entries and zero row sums
nodes.description: Lemma 2 proves high-pass filtering requires negative off-diagonal entries and zero row sums, placing it entirely outside the simplex; Proposition 3 shows TOA realizes these via 'negative mass' in M2.

nodes.name: Case C: latent factor demixing fails simplex membership on three counts
nodes.description: Lemma 3 establishes that for generic mixing matrices, the MMSE demixing projection fails simplex membership via non-unit row sums, non-binary diagonals, and negative entries; Proposition 4 proves TOA can represent these channel-wise projections.

nodes.name: Case D: phase drift/time warping requires dynamic operator adaptation
nodes.description: Lemma 4 proves softmax cannot adapt to the dynamic family of operators needed across varying signal scales for phase drift/time warping; Proposition 5 shows TOA-Gated successfully routes input to specialized, sign-changing sub-operators.

nodes.name: Case E: local feature dynamics vanish under the 1-vector
nodes.description: Lemma 5 proves the optimal rank-2 quadrature projection onto local atoms vanishes under the 1-vector (violating simplex row-sum=1); Proposition 6 establishes TOA-Gated's localized gating and unconstrained mixer allow triggering specialized signed filters per transient.

nodes.name: All five cases collectively motivate TOA's necessity
nodes.description: Together, these five regimes demonstrate concrete, provable cases where the optimal sequence operator violates the simplex constraint that Proposition 1 shows softmax cannot escape, while TOA is shown to realize each exactly.

nodes.name: Synthetic task with latent time-warping regime
nodes.description: A noisy harmonic superposition with phase drift and high-variance noise is generated, with a latent variable controlling one of three time-warping regimes (stationary, periodic vibrato, quadratic chirp), used to validate the theoretical simplex-constraint claims.

nodes.name: Severe capacity bottleneck imposed to isolate architectural efficiency
nodes.description: A severe capacity bottleneck (2 layers, 2 heads) is imposed when comparing TOA-Gated, TOA-ReLU, and Softmax Attention, to rigorously isolate architectural efficiency rather than raw capacity.

nodes.name: TOA-Gated achieves lowest MSE, softmax attention worst
nodes.description: TOA-Gated achieves the lowest MSE (0.0028), outperforming TOA-ReLU (0.0035) and decisively beating Softmax Attention (0.0972).

nodes.name: Learned operator visualizations confirm theoretical predictions
nodes.description: Softmax Attention collapses into low-pass vertical-stripe operators as predicted by Proposition 1; TOA-ReLU learns negative weights via M2 but its static capacity forces destructive interference across warping regimes; TOA-Gated dynamically routes inputs to regime-specific sub-operators, yielding cleanly separated filters.

nodes.name: Demonstrates necessity of unconstrained, sample-adaptive mixing
nodes.description: The synthetic results together demonstrate the necessity of unconstrained, sample-adaptive sequence mixing (i.e., TOA-Gated's design) beyond either fixed simplex-constrained attention or static unconstrained mixing.

nodes.name: TOA integrated into DUET, PatchTST, iTransformer across nine datasets
nodes.description: TOA is evaluated by integrating it into state-of-the-art forecasting backbones (DUET, PatchTST, iTransformer) across nine long-term-forecasting datasets, plus PEMS for short-term forecasting (Table 1-3).

nodes.name: TOA yields consistent gains across backbones
nodes.description: Integrating the gated sequence-mixing operator yields consistent gains across backbones and datasets in both long-term (Table 3) and short-term/PEMS (Table 2) forecasting.

nodes.name: TOA captures high-frequency transients that softmax over-smooths
nodes.description: By bypassing the normalization bottleneck of standard attention, TOA successfully captures rapid, high-frequency transients that similarity-based mechanisms typically over-smooth.

nodes.name: TOA-ReLU and TOA-Gated significantly outperform softmax on UEA
nodes.description: On 28 diverse UEA multivariate classification datasets, TOA-ReLU (69.13%) and TOA-Gated (69.16%) significantly outperform the Softmax baseline (65.62%), with far better average rank and win/tie/loss counts (Table 4).

nodes.name: TOA-Softmax ablation fails to improve, validating necessity of breaking simplex
nodes.description: The TOA-Softmax ablation (64.80%) fails to improve over the softmax baseline, validating that breaking the simplex constraint (not merely adding S1/S2 degrees of freedom under softmax) is necessary for optimal temporal routing.

nodes.name: Dynamic routing enables sample-adaptive feature extraction
nodes.description: By utilizing dynamic routing, TOA functions as a sample-adaptive feature extractor capable of identifying discriminant temporal patterns regardless of the data profile.

nodes.name: TOA-integrated backbones improve F1 across all five benchmarks
nodes.description: TOA-integrated backbones achieve consistent F1-score improvements across all five anomaly detection benchmarks (PSM, MSL, SMAP, SMD, SWAT) (Table 5).

nodes.name: Unconstrained operators eliminate spectral dampening of transients
nodes.description: By replacing row-normalized similarity transport with explicit, unconstrained sequence operators, the method eliminates the spectral dampening that often obscures transient events in standard attention, enabling sharper reconstruction errors for sparse anomalies.

nodes.name: TOA-Gated further optimizes via dynamic noise routing
nodes.description: TOA-Gated further optimizes detection by dynamically routing out noise, delivering precise and reliable detection across diverse domains.

nodes.name: Dense operators risk overfitting on noisy finite-horizon data
nodes.description: Deploying dense N×N matrices inherently increases the risk of overfitting, particularly on noisy, finite-horizon time series, motivating the SOR ablation study on the PatchTST backbone.

nodes.name: SOR yields substantial gains on most datasets
nodes.description: Adding SOR yields substantial gains, prominently on ETTh2 for TOA-ReLU (0.381→0.354) and ETTm2 for TOA-Gated (0.271→0.259), despite a marginal regression on ETTm1 (+0.003) (Table 6).

nodes.name: Confirms hypothesis that unconstrained operators are overfitting-prone
nodes.description: The overall trend confirms the hypothesis that unconstrained explicit operators are prone to overfitting on noisy data, and SOR acts as a vital structural constraint ensuring learned sequence mixers remain generalizable.

isolated_nodes.name: Three tokenization schemes considered
isolated_nodes.description: The formal analysis considers point tokenization (N=L per time step), patch tokenization (PatchTST-style, N=⌊L/p⌋), and inverted tokenization (iTransformer-style, N=C per variate).

isolated_nodes.name: Complementary attention-rank-degeneration literature
isolated_nodes.description: The paper's perspective is noted as complementary to prior analyses showing pure attention layers exhibit a bias toward token uniformity and rank degeneration absent residual and MLP pathways.

isolated_nodes.name: Related sequence-mixing primitives
isolated_nodes.description: Prior work includes static input-independent mixers (TSMixer, DLinear), input-conditioned dynamic-weight approaches (HyperMLP and related fast-weight perspectives, often low-rank/constrained), and efficiency/decomposition/frequency-aware Transformer variants (Informer, Autoformer, FEDformer, LogTrans, ARM) that still use similarity-based aggregation.

isolated_nodes.name: Multi-head aggregation and output projection
isolated_nodes.description: TOA's per-head outputs are concatenated along the feature dimension and linearly projected via a learnable output projection matrix to recover the original embedding dimension, following standard multi-head attention practice.

isolated_nodes.name: Experimental task/backbone/dataset summary
isolated_nodes.description: Evaluation spans long-term forecasting (DUET/PatchTST/iTransformer on Weather, ETT, ECL, Solar, Exchange, Traffic), short-term forecasting (PEMS), anomaly detection (PSM/MSL/SMAP/SMD/SWAT), and classification (28 UEA datasets), as summarized in Table 1.

structural_reasoning: The graph follows one tight theory-to-validation arc. The motivating empirical paradox (C1) is diagnosed as a mismatch between softmax's convex-combination structure and time-series' need for signed operators, formalized as the simplex-constrained mixing bottleneck (C2), further elaborated as an incompleteness in attention's dynamic-MLP-mixer interpretation (C3). This directly motivates TOA's S1/S2 sandwiching construction (C4), stabilized by Stochastic Operator Regularization (C5), and instantiated as three activation variants forming a deliberate ablation ladder (C6: Softmax ⊂ ReLU ⊂ Gated, each addressing a limitation of the previous). The theoretical core is a formal impossibility proof (C7: Proposition 1) which is then applied to five concrete, individually-proven regimes where optimal operators provably violate the simplex constraint (C8) — this is the crux linking the abstract bottleneck to constructive necessity claims. Every downstream empirical section validates a piece of this theory: the synthetic experiment (C9) directly visualizes and quantifies the Proposition-1-predicted failure mode and TOA's escape from it; forecasting (C10), classification (C11), and anomaly detection (C12) results each confirm the practical benefit of breaking the simplex constraint (with C11's TOA-Softmax ablation directly testing and confirming the C6 ablation-ladder logic); and the SOR ablation (C13) validates the C5 regularization design in isolation. Tokenization schemes, related-work contrasts, and experimental setup summaries are treated as isolated/contextual nodes since they support scope and comparison rather than being embedded in the theory-to-validation chain.
